canberra.title: 16 year old fell pregnant during middle-aged rapist’s vile abuse
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual violence. A young girl became pregnant by a middle-aged man while he repeatedly sexually v...
canberra.content:
The now-51-year-old man has been sentenced to five years in jail by the ACT Supreme Court. Photo: John Lomnicki.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual violence.

A young girl became pregnant by a middle-aged man while he repeatedly sexually violated her, despite knowing her age, as he originally met her while she was still wearing her school uniform.

The man, who isn’t named to protect the girl’s identity, was sentenced to five years’ jail with three years’ non-parole, according to a recently published decision from the ACT Supreme Court.

Chief Justice Lucy McCallum said the 16-year-old girl was wearing her school uniform at the end of a school day when she first met the then-44-year-old man at a Canberra shopping centre in 2019.

She asked him to buy her cigarettes, and he did, but then he told her he sold marijuana, so they exchanged phone numbers.

The girl was wearing her uniform when she went to his home during a school day and they smoked the drug, which made her feel sick and throw up. Despite this, he started taking off her clothes.

“Stop. I don’t want to do this. I’m only 16,” she told him.

The man still raped her. He told her not to tell anyone, saying no one would believe her and people would think she was disgusting due to how old he was.

They had sex five more times over the next couple of weeks, even though the girl said she didn’t want to. She said she was buying marijuana from him then smoking it, so thought if she didn’t do what he said, then he would go to her school and tell them what she was doing.

Chief Justice McCallum said she was satisfied the girl would not have had sex with the man on any of these later occasions had she not felt trapped in that way.

The girl also became pregnant during those weeks. The man told her to get an abortion, but she chose to keep her child.

“You stole the joy that should come with a positive pregnancy test … The happiness of becoming a first-time mother was replaced with sadness, confusion, anger and guilt,” the girl went on to tell the man in court.

“My mind was flooded with thoughts no teenager should ever have to face. I wondered how I would explain this to my daughter, whether she would hate me, or whether she would understand.

“You are not a father. You are a predator who tried to gain power through a child.”

Chief Justice McCallum said the girl’s words showed the strength of the impressive young woman, who had demonstrated “extraordinary courage and resilience”.

In 2023, the girl’s partner had asked her to call the man so he could confront him about the abuse. During the call, the man told the pair, “Do you really believe anyone’s going to believe you after all these years?”

Chief Justice McCallum said this “callous remark” confirmed the man’s “complete absence of remorse”.

The man, who is now aged 51, was found guilty of a charge of sexual intercourse without consent at the end of a Supreme Court jury trial earlier this year.

The chief justice said the girl was an intelligent, careful and entirely credible witness, who made it very clear that she did not want to have sex with him.

“His conduct was opportunistic and predatory,” she said.

With time served, the man will be eligible for parole in July 2029.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to police by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

canberra.title: Trump pulls the plug on livestream execution plans
canberra.snippet: The United States government will not livestream the execution by military firing squad of former US Army major and psychiatrist Nidal Ha...
canberra.content:
Nidal Hasan is due to be executed by a military firing squad in the US on 3 December. Photo: Bell County Sheriff’s Department.

The United States government will not livestream the execution by military firing squad of former US Army major and psychiatrist Nidal Hasan, despite having very recently said it would.

The turnaround follows condemnation from around the world for even suggesting the public would want to watch the execution.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had said he wanted the killing to be livestreamed to serve as a deterrent for mass murder. Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed soldiers and injured another 32 in a crowded medical building on a US military base in Texas in 2009.

US President Donald Trump says he was OK with the idea of a publicly streamed execution, which is scheduled for 3 December. However, Vice President JD Vance downplayed the idea and made it clear he wouldn’t watch it if the livestream went ahead.

Numerous Republicans and Democrats in the US loudly objected to the plan.

Issues raised ranged from it being a barbaric move to concerns that images from the broadcasts could be used to fuel radicalisation.

A group of 72 retired US generals, admirals, and military officers published an open letter urging the government to scrap its livestream plans.

They argued that livestreaming would violate constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment, turn a solemn punishment into a “carnival for the enjoyment of voyeurs and spectators”, and transform Hasan into a martyr.

Globally, the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights warned that broadcasting the execution online would breach the prohibition of torture.

And a string of global leaders described the plans as “abhorrent”.

Anthony Albanese was among those critical of the decision, but he said it would not be easy to block Australian viewers from broadcasting the execution.

The Prime Minister instead urged social media platforms not to air it, saying they had a moral obligation to block the streaming.

“I think anybody broadcasting this will damage their own reputations as well,” he said.

“They have a social responsibility here to do the right thing.”

The Australian Greens demanded the Federal Government make it illegal for social media companies to broadcast the killing to Australian viewers.

Greens Senator Sarah Hanson-Young wrote to Communications Minister Anika Wells and eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant, seeking assurance that Australians will not be able to access the execution, whether on streaming services, online platforms or television.

MPs and senators across the political spectrum in Australia condemned the plans.

One Nation’s Barnaby Joyce also strongly opposed the plan.

“This is Roman amphitheatre stuff. No, I don’t agree with that,” he said.

“We don’t have the death penalty in Australia, and I certainly don’t want children, or anyone for that matter, witnessing another human being shot by a firing squad.”

The eSafety Commissioner, however, said the government would not be able to legally prevent social media platforms from showing the footage.

Amid global and US domestic backlash to the livestream plan, Mr Trump has scrapped the idea.

In a social media post overnight on Thursday (15 October), Australian time, the President said: “Many very good and well-meaning people would rather not watch him die …

“[It] might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan.”

Mr Trump said the execution would still be viewed live in person by immediate families of the victims “if they so choose”.

Australia’s Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy was the first government minister to react to the news when asked about it on ABC News Breakfast Friday morning.

“I’m very relieved that this execution will not be live streamed,” he said.

“Like most Australians, I believe there is no place for the depictions of these sorts of incidents on the internet.”

canberra.title: ACT public schools face another week of disruptions as teachers demand staffing guarantees
canberra.snippet: ACT public schools will face another round of disruptions next week, with one-hour work stoppages planned across the city from Monday, 19...
canberra.content:
ACT schools set to face another round of disruption with planned industrial action by the teachers’ union from 19 to 23 October. Photo: James Coleman.

ACT public schools will face another round of disruptions next week, with one-hour work stoppages planned across the city from Monday, 19 October, to Friday, 23 October, as the Australian Education Union (AEU) steps up pressure on the ACT Government to guarantee adequate staffing levels.

The rolling stoppages, between 8:30 am and 9:30 am, will affect different schools each day, with reduced supervision, delayed preschool starts and possible cancellations of camps and excursions.

It will be the fourth round of work stoppages this year, following a two-hour stoppage on 24 September, when AEU members distributed pamphlets across Canberra to highlight deteriorating working conditions.

The latest action comes amid reports of severe staffing pressures in public schools, including a teacher being asked to supervise a class of 90 students and parents being warned that normal learning arrangements could not be maintained for several days because of staff illness and other absences.

A Canberra public school teacher, speaking to Region on condition of anonymity, said the Education Directorate had failed to establish an effective system for finding replacement teachers.

According to the teacher, there was no centralised app or formal system to manage staff absences, leaving schools scrambling whenever a teacher was unavailable.

The teacher said the resulting uncertainty added pressure to already stretched staff and disrupted students’ learning.

Under the latest arrangements, parents are being encouraged to keep their children at home until 9:30 am on the day their school is affected.

Primary school students who need to attend will have minimal supervision, but preschools will remain closed during stoppages because of staffing ratios and supervision requirements.

Before-school care services will operate as usual, but preschool children attending those services must be collected when care ends if the school has not yet reopened.

School bus services, including Supported School Transport for eligible students, will continue operating at their usual times because Transport Canberra cannot adjust schedules to accommodate the delayed starts.

Some school camps and excursions may also need to be cancelled or rescheduled, with affected families to be contacted directly.

AEU members, including school leaders, teachers, school psychologists and learning support assistants, will gather at prominent locations across Canberra throughout the week.

The campaign will begin in Gungahlin on Monday, followed by Belconnen on Tuesday, the Inner North and Inner South on Wednesday, Weston and Woden on Thursday, and Tuggeranong on Friday.

AEU ACT branch president Angela Burroughs said the union wanted the community to understand what was at stake.

“Educators are out in the community because the government has not yet made the commitments at the bargaining table that our schools need,” Ms Burroughs said.

“The ACT must resource its public education system appropriately. That starts with a real, enforceable guarantee on staffing levels.”

She said staffing shortages were affecting the quality of education, student and staff safety, and wellbeing.

“When schools don’t have the staff they need, students miss out, workloads blow out, and people are put at risk. Our members are tired of filling the gaps with their own time and goodwill.”

The union is demanding a staffing guarantee based on what individual schools need to operate safely and effectively, rather than what government budgets allocate.

Ms Burroughs also challenged Education Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith to match her ambition for public education with concrete commitments.

“Minister Stephen-Smith says she wants public education to be the first choice for all Canberrans. Our members need to see the commitment to make that a reality. Parents choose a school when they trust it will be properly staffed. The government can build that trust by delivering a guarantee at the table.”

AEU ACT branch secretary Patrick Judge said members were showing an unprecedented level of commitment to the campaign.

“Educators are not asking for anything extravagant. We’re asking for the staffing that makes schools safe and lets students learn. The government has the power to resolve this, and we demand real change,” Mr Judge said.

The union has encouraged parents and community members to meet educators at the daily gatherings and support their campaign.

The Education Directorate has published a list of affected schools, times and dates.

canberra.title: Canberra streets turn rainbow for SpringOUT’s 27th year
canberra.snippet: Canberra’s pride festival, SpringOUT, is about to return for its 27th year with its biggest calendar of events ever. This year&#821...
canberra.content:
SpringOUT Pride Festival is back in 2026 with a five-week program starting soon. Photo: SpringOUT.

Canberra’s pride festival, SpringOUT, is about to return for its 27th year with its biggest calendar of events ever.

This year’s programming has been extended from four to five weeks to include the unveiling of a new portrait of Australia’s own drag queen Courtney Act at the National Portrait Gallery, which launches on Friday 23 October, and will be followed by a Q&A with LGBTQIA+ artist Paul Yore.

Courtney Act appeared on the first season of Australian Idol in 2003, before competing in RuPaul’s Drag Race and Big Brother UK. She has also released several albums while also serving as a major advocate for the Sydney Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras.

SpringOUT’s traditional festivities begin on Saturday 31 October with the popular free, family event Fair Day at Glebe Park.

The event will be stacked with local performers including Jett Blyton, Etcetera Etcetera, Stella Eve and plenty of other local LGBTQIA+ talent.

Festival Director Danny Corvini said the organisers for this year’s festival had done a lot of work to ensure as many people as possible feel included.

“Our biggest event is Fair Day in Glebe Park, which is an all-day event with over 80 stalls, food trucks and entertainment sections. While that naturally is quite an exciting and overstimulating time, one thing we’re really focusing on is having quiet sections and more relaxed parts of the park,” he said.

“Our community has told us that there is more of a demand for quiet spaces.

“Not everyone wants to be on a dance floor or in a mosh pit. We are definitely catering to that this year with two dedicated quiet spaces at Fair Day, which is otherwise quite a festival atmosphere.”

Several other events, including a comedy gala, pride sports at Lyneham Sports Precinct, and a one-night-only performance from Mary Kinani at Fiction, round out a stacked festival.

Mr Corvini said the festival had continued to grow in support every year, with Canberrans showing they were amongst the most inclusive people in the country.

“Within SpringOUT, we thought last year was a huge festival. This year it’s only getting bigger,” he said.

“With next year being the 10th anniversary of marriage equality in Australia, it’s looking to be even bigger still.

“I think the reason we see this support here is that Canberrans in general are more laid-back with a more progressive mentality than most other parts of the country. That all lends to supporting people who are LGBTQIA+.”

Mr Corvini said he would like people to attend as many of the events across the festival as possible with an open mind.

“Our theme this year is ‘Be Yourself’,” he said.

“That epitomises everything the festival is about. The world can be a scary place, and that’s not just exclusive to members of the LGBTQIA+ community.

“We want people to be themselves, have fun and do it respectfully. Whether you’re on the LGBTQIA+ spectrum or an ally, we want people to come by and have fun.”

SpringOUT runs from 23 October to 1 December 2026. To see the full calendar of events, visit the festival website here.

canberra.title: Here’s an idea from left field: make the ACT a low-tax honeypot
canberra.snippet: The ACT should review all its taxes and charges against other states and consider cutting them to gain a competitive edge to attract inve...
canberra.content:
UC Vice-Chancellor Bill Shorten says the ACT could try being more competitive on taxes. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

The ACT should review all its taxes and charges against other states and consider cutting them to gain a competitive edge to attract investment. That suggestion came from an unlikely source at a Canberra Business Chamber event at the Hyatt on Thursday.

Labor luminary and now University of Canberra Vice-Chancellor Bill Shorten told the Grow the Pie event, in response to a question about how the ACT Government could boost the Territory economy, that it could “Delaware” it, referring to the north-eastern US state with a low-tax, business-friendly regime.

“Why not look at the range of state taxes and charges and go lower,” he said.

“And say to the electorate, we’re going to go live, but if it creates too much debt or if the idea doesn’t work, then we’ll go back and do what we did.

“But see if there’s a way that Canberra can become the most competitive jurisdiction to attract people to come here and create a volume of business activities that might be something else.”

Mr Shorten later said the ACT needed to consider itself more of a city-state than a territory and look to other city-states such as Singapore to see where it could leverage its advantages and differentiate itself.

He said it was just an idea for now but indicated the university would flesh it out over time.

In a risk-averse political environment, this approach would be challenging, “but sometimes going bold, going big is not the worst idea in the world”.

“Don’t try and do it all the time, it’s tiring, but I think that maybe look at where Canberra could be competitive on state taxes and charges,” Mr Shorten said.

Mr Shorten also suggested that the ACT Government needed to slow its capital expenditure or spending on acquiring, maintaining and improving assets.

He said it was good to have things, but not if you can’t pay for them or if they attract too much interest.

Which prompted a response from event host David Speers: “Just checking, you’re from the Labor Party?”

“No, I’m from UC!” Mr Shorten replied.

The ACT’s size also drove Mr Shorten’s push for UC and the Canberra Institute of Technology to merge, saying a jurisdiction the size of the Territory could not afford two different post-school education systems.

He said it was a no-brainer that would create jobs and grow the number of students in the ACT.

“At the moment, CIT has about 16 per cent of all VET enrolments in Canberra. That’s too low,” Mr Shorten said.

That was partly because CIT didn’t have the capacity to offer all the courses it should.

Mr Shorten said some in the TAFE sector worry about their identity but “what’s going to kill your identity is if you run out of money you become insolvent”.

“As the need for skills and knowledge changes, as the Federal Government says that they’re doing what’s called tertiary harmonisation, as I think parents want to make sure their kids get the best start in life, and employers need to deal with the shortages, especially with some of this immigration stuff keeps rolling on, and there’s this race to the bottom, then we’re going to need the most agile post-school educational skills learning possible,” he said.

At an event where regulation and red tape were highlighted as impediments to business, Mr Shorten blasted the ‘regulation’ imposed on universities related to international students as economic self-harm.

He recognised that the student visa system needed tightening, but the current debate risked killing Australia’s fourth-largest export industry.

“We are sending a very mixed message to our region,” he said.

“Between 2005 and 2025, this country has educated 4.3 million citizens of other countries, and the vast bulk of them have gone home.

“Every international student we say we don’t want here, we are flushing $70,000 net down the toilet in the Australian economy.”

The ACT Government says higher education is the Territory’s largest export industry and worth $1 billion a year to the local economy.

australia.title: Greens leader denies knowledge of ‘secret dossier’ on how to handle Jordon Steele-John misconduct allegations
australia.snippet: David Shoebridge says 47-page document not ‘made by, used by, or seen by’ his office as matter referred to parliamentary standards commis...
australia.content:
Greens leader David Shoebridge has denied knowledge of the existence of an alleged crisis management document on how to deal with allegations against Jordon Steele-John being made public.

The Nine newspapers reported on Friday afternoon the existence of a “secret dossier”, first drafted in 2016, which contained misconduct allegations against the Western Australian Greens senator and how to suppress their media coverage.

Guardian Australia has not independently confirmed the document’s contents.

In a statement responding to claims that the federal leader’s office had access to the 47-page document, Shoebridge said it was not “made by, used by, or seen by the leader’s office”.

“The office is committed to having the matters comprehensively investigated with a fair, independent and timely process,” he said.

“Everyone deserves a safe workplace, and all complaints should be considered in a fair and robust process.”

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

The WA Greens confirmed the existence of the document and said it was created in response to allegations first made against the senator in 2016.

“The Greens WA responded to allegations about Jordon Steele-John in 2016. The allegations were not substantiated and the named persons have never lodged a formal complaint,” the statement said.

“Reference has been made to an internal document that has been provided to the media. This document outlines the management of communications about this matter.”

Steele-John confirmed he would leave the party room on Thursday after some details of historical complaints about inappropriate comments made to women ranging between 2017 and 2025 were publicly aired in the media.

The 32-year-old senator rejected the claims and said he had referred them to the Western Australian Greens for a “fair, independent process” that “upholds the principles of natural justice and ensures procedural fairness for everyone involved”.

“I utterly reject this characterisation of me, which tries to assert I am someone I am not,” Steele-John said in a statement.

Shoebridge told ABC on Friday morning he referred the complaints outlined in a letter to the parliamentary workplace support service (PWSS), which he said was “unable to deal with it because of the circumstances and nature of the allegation”.

The PWSS’s chief executive, Leonie McGregor, said the office had not been given the letter but had provided Shoebridge’s office with options, including referring the complaints to the independent parliamentary standards commission (IPSC).

Guardian Australia understands Shoebridge has now referred the matter to the IPSC.

The WA Greens confirmed on Thursday they would “seek legal advice on how best to establish an independent inquiry” into the matters raised.

A statement from the co-conveners, Giz Watson and Simone Collins, and state director, Dean Smith, said: “Our party is built on the contributions of members, volunteers, staff and supporters, and every one of them deserves to feel safe and respected when they take part in our work. Maintaining that safety is a responsibility we hold seriously.”

Shoebridge confirmed Steele-John would not return to parliament until the independent investigations had been completed.

“It’s my understanding that leave means leave,” he told ABC.

“I have responsibility for the party room and the Greens’ functions, and I have some capacity to direct in relation to the party room. But Senator Steele-John has indicated to me that he’s on leave, and that leave means leave.”

australia.title: Elizabeth Struhs’ child protection case not ‘prioritised’ due to high workload, inquest hears
australia.snippet: Eight-year-old Queensland girl died in 2022 after being denied insulin by her religious parents Get our breaking news email , free app or...
australia.content:
Elizabeth Struhs’ child protection case was not “prioritised” or worked intensively because the staff member assigned to her case was “very busy”, a coroner has heard.

The Queensland coroner’s court also heard the case worker may have been “overly influenced” by the presentation of Struhs’ “upper class home”, putting cases believed to involve a more immediate risk ahead of Elizabeth’s.

The eight-year-old died on 7 January 2022 of diabetic ketoacidosis, after her father, Jason Struhs, stopped providing insulin to treat her type 1 diabetes at their home in Toowoomba, Queensland. A long-term sceptic of his wife’s beliefs, he had converted to them and joined her religious sect – which subscribed to an extreme form of Christianity and denied the use of medicine – in 2021.

Coroner Ainslie Kirkegaard is holding an inquest into Elizabeth’s death. She has previously heard the eight-year-old came to the attention of child safety after a 2019 incident where she presented to hospital in a coma.

Child safety ended its involvement with the family after just 17 weeks of what was supposed to be an intensive intervention, assessing her as “safe”.

But the single child safety officer assigned to Elizabeth’s case told the court on Friday her approach wasn’t intensive and she didn’t make weekly check-ins during that period, despite departmental guidelines.

The department chose to release her back into Jason’s sole care over the objections of specialist doctors who treated Elizabeth in Brisbane, subject to a voluntary intervention with parental agreement (IPA).

The coroner heard just a single child safety officer was assigned to the case, and would often conduct home visits alone.

The officer gave evidence on Friday.

“Ideally I wanted to visit with the family at least once a week, in accordance with our IPAT (intervention with parental agreement team) guidelines,” according to her statement, presented to the court.

“During my management of the IPA for the Struhs family, I recall that I was not always available to conduct home visits with the family. I recall this being a very busy time for the CSSC (child safety service centre) and I also recall being regularly out of the office travelling to visit other families.

“I note that one of the home visits to the Struhs family was conducted by a student who was working in the team at the time.”

She said Elizabeth’s case wasn’t treated as a complex case, which it should have been due to the intervention.

But at the time, she had a “big caseload” – approximately 25-28 children in 15 families on the same intervention– she said. The coroner has previously heard that the Toowoomba region was among the busiest in the state for child safety.

Counsel assisting Simon Hamlyn-Harris said most of them were experiencing significant domestic violence, drug use, sexual abuse and it was not often that she was required to work with “upper class families” like the Struhs.

The case worker agreed that she may have been “overly influenced” by the presentation of the Struhs home.

“I believe that we may have prioritised other cases at the time for children who were presenting at more immediate risk,” she told the court.

She also told the court that she may have had a bias because her own child had nearly died of type 1 diabetes at age 6. She had asked not to be assigned to the case, she said.

Several witnesses have previously told the coroner they expected the intervention to last months or a year, but the case worker said they were supposed to not last longer than three months, because they were an intensive approach.

On Friday, Kirkegaard asked another child safety witness whether they felt “organisational pressure to get a matter like this finalised quickly”.

“Absolutely,” the witness said, adding an IPA could be intrusive and potentially harmful to a child if dragged out.

“I don’t believe it impacted our decision making,” she said.

On 13 November 2019, a more senior child safety officer assessed Elizabeth as “safe” and the intervention was ended.

The case worker told the coroner on Friday that she hadn’t appreciated the danger of Elizabeth’s mother’s church group, which was considered a source of support for the family.

All 14 adult members of the sect – known as the Saints – were convicted of Elizabeth’s manslaughter last year, including Elizabeth’s parents, Kerrie and Jason, and the group leader, Brendan Stevens.

In her statement she said Jason had agreed to continue to treat his daughter against his wife’s beliefs and that she had “faith” that should Kerrie stand in the way he would leave her.

None of the witnesses can be identified for legal reasons.

The inquest continues.

australia.title: One Nation proposes $2,000 baby subsidy in Victoria but says it won’t touch state abortion laws
australia.snippet: Announcement comes a day after Liberal and Labor parties say they will cover out-of-pocket costs for abortion care Get our new political ...
australia.content:
One Nation has proposed a $2,000 baby bonus for new parents in Victoria – a day after the Labor and Liberal parties both agreed to cover out-of-pocket costs for abortion care.

The deputy leader of One Nation in Victoria, Colleen Harkin, announced the plan on Friday to remove out-of-pocket costs for pregnant women in the public healthcare system and a $2,000 subsidy for those accessing private maternity care.

She said it would cost $136m over four years but admitted it was a “ballpark” figure that would depend on how many babies were born each year.

“We don’t go hard on figures, because we actually don’t have access to the detail of this stuff,” Harkin told reporters.

She said One Nation “will not touch the abortion laws” in Victoria despite the federal party’s national platform pledging to “seek every opportunity to roll back brutal and extreme abortion law”.

“We have no state abortion policy because it is not our focus whatsoever,” Harkin said, accusing the Labor party of “lying” and “engaging with really cheap American-style scaremongering”.

On Thursday, Labor announced that, if re-elected in November, it would eliminate out-of-pocket costs for abortion care, costing $30m over four years, and claimed One Nation could use abortion as a negotiating chip with the Coalition in the event of a hung parliament.

Under Labor’s plan, private providers would be paid to deliver medical and surgical abortions up to 16 weeks’ gestation. Women would no longer have to pay for GP and specialist consultations, scans, tests or medication, which can cost up to $1,000. Those in regional Victoria who must travel long distances for care would also be eligible for a subsidy.

The government would extend access to medical abortion from nine to 10 weeks’ gestation, while commissioning a clinical review into whether it could safely be offered at up to 12 weeks’ gestation.

Within hours the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, said the Coalition would match the plan to cover out-of-pocket costs and the travel subsidy. In a statement she said “the Liberals and Nationals will not allow Labor to play politics on this issue”.

On Friday, Fiona Carroll, the wife of the premier, Ben Carroll, defended her husband for raising abortion in the leadup to the election.

“It does build on the Labor legacy, and I don’t think I’m politicising this because it is fundamental to the women in this state,” she said.

Fiona said it was “even better” the Coalition had matched the commitment, as it would “take some of that fear” out of the election for women.

Neither the Liberal party nor Labor responded to a request for comment on One Nation’s policy.

Anti-abortion activist Joanna Howe criticised Wilson, describing the Liberals as being in “lock step with Labor on every vile and evil policy” and directing her followers in Victoria to back One Nation. The Australian Christian Lobby’s Victorian director, Jasmine Yeun, said it was “getting more difficult to vote for a major party”.

But the chief executive of Women’s Health Victoria, Sally Hasler, welcomed the bipartisanship on the issue. It means no matter who is elected, Victoria will become the first state to provide abortion free.

“We are very reassured to know that it won’t be an election issue because we have support from both the ALP and the Coalition to not just protect rights but to expand rights,” Hasler said.

She described One Nation’s announcement as a deliberate attempt to frame reproductive healthcare as a choice between abortion and maternity care.

“Responding to an abortion care announcement with a maternity care announcement is a false trade-off, and it’s a deliberate one,” she said.

“It is a well-played move from the international anti-rights agenda to wind back women’s rights – one which narrowly defines women’s reproductive health.”

australia.title: Exclusive Brethren head denies knowing church members were volunteering for Liberal party during 2025 election
australia.snippet: Bruce Hales also denies church was a cult while son tells parliamentary committee it was ‘a bit rough’ being labelled as such Get our bre...
australia.content:
The most senior member of the Exclusive Brethren has denied any knowledge of or involvement in thousands of members from his church volunteering for the Liberal party at the 2025 election.

The Plymouth Brethren christian church has rejected claims it coordinated volunteers and a campaign for the Coalition, and that it secretly paid far-right figures to stage stunts against the prime minister and other Labor MPs.

The fiery parliamentary committee hearing on Friday was marred by clashes, with members of the committee accusing one another of “religious persecution” and “running a protection racket” for the church.

Bruce Hales, the Brethren’s most senior member, said he had no involvement or knowledge of church members volunteering for the Coalition.

“I want to be clear and unequivocal. I had no involvement whatsoever in relation to any members who volunteered or took part in any aspect of the 2025 federal election,” he told the inquiry.

“I did not plan such activities. I did not coordinate such activities. I did not direct such activities. I did not fund such activities.”

Hales denied that his church was a cult, a term used by the prime minister, while his son, Gareth Hales, who also appeared before the committee, said it was “a bit rough” being labelled as such.

Gareth Hales gave evidence on Friday he had met Morgan C Jonas and Chris de Bruyne separately in a business capacity, and briefly discussed the “general direction the government was headed”. The independent MP Andrew Gee referred to the two as far-right activists, although Gareth Hales denied knowing their political affiliations at the time.

Nine newspapers have reported Jonas and de Bruyne were involved in a campaign that targeted Labor and other left-leaning politicians during the election. Gareth Hales denied reports his company Sante Global paid the two men to disrupt other campaigns.

There was turmoil in the committee as Coalition members likened questioning by Labor and crossbench MPs to a “Spanish Inquisition”.

Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie and Liberal MP Ben Small repeatedly interrupted questions, calling them “disgraceful” and “disrespectful”. McKenzie said the line of questioning looked “a lot like religious persecution”, while Small was accused of trying to answer questions for the church.

Gee, who was previously a Nationals MP, said the two were running an “old Liberal party protection racket”, a comment he was forced to withdraw.

On 20 April 2025, just under two weeks before the federal election, Bruce Hales gave a sermon where he told members to be “fervent in prayer for good government”, and that the country needed to be happy again and smiling again.

The latter two phrases were seen on posters endorsing the Liberal party during the campaign. Bruce Hales denied his sermon was a call to action and said he had no knowledge of his words being used in billboards and advertising at the election.

Nine newspapers reported the sermon had been broadcast and then turned into a text message by Gareth Hale and his brothers, which said, “We need to make sure our booths are manned and our volunteers are fired up.”

Gareth Hales, who has no official role in the church, said he could not confirm or deny whether he had written this message but denied instructing members to join the campaign. He said he had encouraged members who had already been volunteering to “keep doing what they were doing”.

Gee, who claimed he was tailed by several Brethren members in his regional New South Wales electorate, said it “defies belief” that the church had no role in coordinating volunteers.

Gareth Hales said they were not acting as members of the church.

“I can understand it’s difficult to believe but they weren’t members of the church, they were members of concerned business groups and members of private citizens – they weren’t there on behalf of the church,” Gareth Hales said.

Gee replied: “I, for one, am not buying what you are selling but I do appreciate you giving evidence today.”

australia.title: MPs clash over grilling of Exclusive Brethren leader on alleged election campaigning – video
australia.snippet: Exclusive Brethren leader Bruce Hales denies any role in coordinating church members’ campaigning for the Liberals during the 2025 federa...
australia.content:
Exclusive Brethren leader Bruce Hales denies any role in coordinating church members’ campaigning for the Liberals during the 2025 federal election, telling a parliamentary inquiry he had ‘no knowledge’ of the events and ‘no part in planning them’. Hales says his sons may have deliberately kept him in the dark, saying it was ‘quite likely’ they had not sought his permission, as MPs grilled him over members’ presence at polling booths and ‘Make Australia smile again’ campaign signage

  • Brethren church denies paying far-right activists to stage election stunts targeting Albanese and others

world.title: LGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrested
world.snippet: At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports Mass arrests, forced ...
world.content:
Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report.

More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network, an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status.

The intensifying crackdown comes as the law criminalising homosexuality in the country was toughened earlier this year. On 11 March, Senegal’s parliament amended the penal code, doubling the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex relations to 10 years.

The new law introduced penalties of up to seven years in prison and a fine of 500,000 to 5m CFA francs (£650–£6,500) for promoting homosexuality, or supporting or financing LGBTQ+ people and organisations.

Larissa Kojoué, LGBTQ+ rights researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “LGBTQ+ people are being forced to curb their normal activities … for fear of arrest and increased stigma. Senegal’s government should call a halt to this crackdown, which threatens everyone’s rights.”

Same-sex sexual activity was criminalised in Senegal in 1965, but hostility towards LGBTQ+ individuals has grown in recent years. During the 2024 presidential campaign, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, who ended up winning the election, and the former prime minister Ousmane Sonko promised to strengthen laws criminalising same-sex relations, framing the issue as a national priority.

Arrests of men and women have happened all over the country. The police say they have arrested people based on information extracted from seized phones, third-party allegations or raids on private premises.

The changes to the penal code have had a chilling effect on lawyers, who said they were afraid to represent people for fear of being prosecuted themselves, according to the report. Doctors told Human Rights Watch that the changes were discouraging people from seeking HIV testing and treatment.

While there was a 49% fall in new HIV infections in western and central Africa from 2010 to 2022, sub-Saharan Africa remains disproportionately affected by the virus, with 64% of all people living with HIV globally.

Sylvie Beaumont, a consultant with HIV Justice Network, said she had received anecdotal evidence that HIV clinics had seen a drop in attendance. “Obviously this is not good for the HIV response because people are going without treatment, they’re not going to get tested,” she said.

“The consequences are really bad and it’s sad because Senegal was a country that was doing well with their HIV response. They are shooting themselves in the foot.”

She said while the law criminalising deliberate HIV transmission was not part of the reforms to the penal code this year, there had been an “unprecedented” rate of arrests in recent months. She labelled the charges “nonsensical” because it was reported that most people had either only discovered their status upon arrest; were arrested with condoms; or were on treatment that renders transmission of the virus impossible.

The report said police had breached confidentiality of ongoing criminal investigations involving suspected LGBTQ+ people by leaking details to the media, which reported personal and confidential information, including HIV status – exposing individuals to social stigma, family rejection, threats and violence.

LGBTQ+ people interviewed by Human Rights Watch said the crackdown was instilling fear among their community, and causing them to feel anxious and depressed. Many have gone into hiding, restricted their movements or relocated; some have left the country.

The report pointed out that the crackdown flew in the face of domestic and international laws that guaranteed the right to a fair trial, privacy and non-discrimination.

The changes to Senegal’s penal code is part of a trend across sub-Saharan Africa towards more punitive legislation directed against LGBTQ+ people.

There have been dozens of arrests in Niger since it criminalised “sexual relations with a person of the same sex” in February. It was the first time in the country’s history that homosexuality had been criminalised, and followed the introduction of similar laws and penal codes in neighbouring Mali and Burkina Faso within the past two years. All three are ruled by military juntas.

In May, Ghana, which already outlaws gay sex, passed legislation criminalising LGBTQ+ “activities”. The bill, which has not been signed into law by the president, is the latest iteration of legislation first proposed in 2021. In 2023, Uganda’s Anti-Homosexuality Act made homosexual acts punishable by death.

world.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza denies using AI to write prize-winning story
world.snippet: Article in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writers The Zimbabwean ...
world.content:
The Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated.

Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter was announced as the winner of the prestigious Caine prize for African writers on 6 October. Five days later, The Atlantic published an article by the author and journalist Vauhini Vara titled: “Yet Another Literary prize winner Seems to Be AI.”

Vara said that she had run the story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The exception, she said, was an epigraph from what is described as an unpublished poem by the South African writer Vangile Gantsho.

Vara said that when she read the story, she “was struck by the proliferation of language that is common in AI-produced writing: the not x, but y sentence constructions; the glut of metaphors; the platitudinous aphorisms”.

She said: “Taste is subjective, but trust me, this story is bad – maudlin and full of tired tropes.”

Kundizeza responded in a statement on X: “For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote ‘The Blue Fighter’. I did not use generative AI to write it. It is entirely my own work.

“I look forward to continuing to work with the Caine prize team, and to celebrating this recognition with the people who helped bring this story into the world. Most importantly, I will continue to write.”

Similar claims have been made recently about other literary prize winners. In July, the Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir won the Commonwealth Foundation’s short story prize with The Serpent in the Grove, despite critics on social media claiming it had “obvious markers” of AI writing.

Last month, the Canadian-Haitian writer Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était Ça Ou Mourir (It Was That or Die) was removed from the longlist of France’s most prestigious literary prize, the Goncourt, after an anonymous online account alleged the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.

The Caine prize said in a statement that it was reviewing the allegations that Kundizeza had used AI. It said: “When such claims are made, it is our responsibility to look into them. We aim to do this by taking a human-centred approach, ensuring that writers are supported and cared for during the process.”

Its chair questioned the reliability of AI-detection software itself.

Ellah Wakatama told the BBC’s Front Row radio show: “As someone who chairs a prize, I’m obviously not against AI, but what I am against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case, regardless of what the Atlantic says, because they have already proclaimed our winner to be a cheater without investigating it properly.

“I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready.”

Vara said in her article, and repeated in an interview with Front Row, that she had read a 2021 story by Kundizeza that was tonally and stylistically different from The Blue Fighter.

In his statement, he responded: “To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing.”

Vara pointed to Pangram’s own research that found that false positives were rare, including for non-native English speakers writing in English, as well as a peer-reviewed journal article that found Pangram had “strong accuracy” when assessing mock academic papers created fully, partly or with no AI. However, she acknowledged to the BBC that there was “relatively little third-party research” on the accuracy of AI detection software.

world.title: Guinea-Bissau denies it has approved controversial vaccine trial in newborns
world.snippet: Health minister says government ‘did not authorize’ Danish-led hepatitis B trial in babies backed by RFK Jr Guinea-Bissau has not approve...
world.content:
Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday.

The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist.

Members of a Danish research ethics committee were informed that officials in Guinea-Bissau had approved an updated design of the study, which influenced some committee members’ votes to proceed with the trial last week.

But the health ministry never agreed to or authorized the trial, said Quinhin Nantote in Portuguese at a press briefing, where he referred to the study as “tests”.

“The ministry did not authorize the tests under the terms presented in the publications currently in circulation,” the health minister said. He said officials in Guinea-Bissau were “surprised” to see media reports that the country had given approval to the study.

“Any scientific research initiative involving human beings, particularly children, ‌must ⁠strictly comply with applicable national legislation, international ethical principles, competent evaluation and approval mechanisms,” Nantote said.

He spoke after convening an emergency meeting in Guinea-Bissau with the Bandim Health Project, the local ethics committee, the National Institute of Public Health (Inasa) and the Expanded Vaccination Program (PAV).

The Bandim Health Project is run by the Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, whose decades of research have been called into question in the past year.

The claims made in nearly all of their papers are “highly misleading”, said Charlotte Strøm, a Danish researcher who has co-authored research showing that Aaby, Stabell Benn, and their co-authors had no significant findings in 24 out of 25 studies and that they’ve chosen not to publish research that may not support their viewpoints.

“When researchers operate like this and abandon proper methodological rigor, they literally decide on the results themselves, and that is not science,” Strøm said, calling it “problematic, questionable [and] unethical”.

She added: “I believe there is serious cause for concern.”

Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, which he says shows that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight”.

Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer did not respond by press time to the Guardian’s questions about why the Danish ethics committee members were told the trial had been approved by local authorities and why it could not be held in Denmark.

In Denmark, infants born to hepatitis B-negative parents do not receive the shot, there is widespread testing for and low incidence of the virus, and the robust healthcare system can track health outcomes and provide timely and comprehensive medical care – making it an ideal location for such a study.

“It’s completely unethical that this trial is even proposed,” because a safe and effective vaccine has been available for decades, said BK Titanji, a researcher at Emory University.

It’s “reassuring” to see Guinea-Bissau pushing back on the trial, Titanji said, adding: “A study like this one needs the highest level of ethical scrutiny. You are going to be conducting a study on the most vulnerable population, which is newborn babies, in a country that is resource-constrained.”

When Titanji recently applied for approval of a collaborative study in Cameroon, she had to include extensive documentation in her application – and it was a survey, not medical research on human subjects, she said. “I can’t come to Emory’s [institutional review board] and just be like: ‘I got permission from Cameroon.’ I have to provide the document.”

The researchers should release these documents and an updated protocol showing how the study would be conducted, she said.

Experts have decried the African experiment as “horribly unethical and cruel”, “neocolonialist” and “damaging”.

“For the government of Guinea-Bissau to stand up against the United States and Denmark exploiting its children is no small statement,” said Colette Delawalla, a researcher and founder and CEO of the non-profit Stand Up for Science. “We absolutely must respect their sovereignty as a nation.”

It would cost approximately $13,200 to buy enough vaccines through Unicef and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, to immunize all newborns in Guinea-Bissau each year, Delawalla pointed out.

Everyone involved should work together to ensure that every baby in Guinea-Bissau receives the birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccination, she added. “This is not muddy water: we can use Black babies to further pseudoscience or we can save children’s lives with a 20-cent shot.”

It is unclear whether the US plans to move forward with the study, even after reporting indicated that the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has again set aside $1.6m for funding for the trial this year, to be matched by private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.

“The ​study has ⁠not been approved,” the HHS told Reuters in a statement. The agency has not responded to the Guardian’s questions about the trial.

At least four members of the Danish committee resigned after approval for the trial was fast-tracked. The rules of the committee had to be changed because randomized controlled trials were outside of its purview. When committee members requested more information about the Guinea-Bissau approval, no further details were provided.

The study would enroll 14,000 newborns in Guinea-Bissau, half of whom would be vaccinated at birth and half of whom would be denied the immunization for the first six weeks of life. Hepatitis B is widespread in the country, and infection in children can have serious lifelong effects.

Guinea-Bissau, which currently has a transitional military government following a coup in November, requested in January a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study. In the meantime, Nantote said at the time, it was “canceled or suspended”.

Other officials in Guinea-Bissau also pushed back on the research. “It’s not going to happen, period,” the foreign minister, João Bernardo Vieira, said in February.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has offered support in rolling out the hepatitis B vaccine at birth to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau. “WHO stands ready to support Guinea‑Bissau as it considers its way forward and in accelerating the introduction of the birth dose and strengthening implementation,” the organization said in a February statement pushing back on the trial.

world.title: Controversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-Bissau
world.snippet: Recommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchers A controversial research trial ...
world.content:
A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.

It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.

At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.

Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”

Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”

Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants in Guinea-Bissau in the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.

An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said was suspended after international uproar earlier this year.

Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.

“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.

Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reportedly set aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.

The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.

The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported by Rolling Stone. This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed.

The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly.

In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus.

Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University in Denmark.

According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries.

The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward.

“It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark.

Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark.

Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer.

The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held a dual appointment with Bandim as recently as December.

Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchers found no effects at all.

This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.”

When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028.

Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”

  • This article was amended on 13 October 2026. A previous version said CIDRAP first reported news that the research trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee. Rolling Stone had actually reported the news first.

world.title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
world.snippet: Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza The Nobel peace...
world.content:
The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.

The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.

“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on the international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.

That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.

“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.

Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.

“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.

“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”

In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.

“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.

“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.

The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded with disbelief.

“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.

“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”

Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.

The ICJ, a UN body, rules on disputes between states, while the international criminal court (ICC) investigates and prosecutes individuals accused of atrocities and other grave international crimes.

Hours after the announcement, the Trump administration unveiled broad new sanctions against the ICC, on which Pillay also once served. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the measures were to ensure the court would never prosecute Americans.

The ICC has not charged any US nationals, and has previously pointed out that it is a court of last resort, unnecessary in the case of countries with effective legal systems. Last year, Donald Trump, who has long coveted the Nobel peace prize, imposed personal sanctions against ICC officials deemed to be involved in investigations of Americans or Israelis. The new sanctions target the court as an institution, blocking any ICC assets in the US and giving US companies and individuals six months to wind down any business with the court.

The ICC said the sanctions were “an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do”.

“It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the court said in a statement.

Pillay’s award was welcomed by human rights activists and hailed in South Africa, home to four previous laureates. The country’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”

Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.

“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.

Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.

“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.

In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.

“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.

Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.

On Friday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”
